idiom_name: type assertion with the comma-ok form: if fl, ok := w.(http.Flusher); ok
implementation_notes: Go turns the query into a type assertion against a consumer-declared interface: `v, ok := x.(I)` reports whether x's dynamic type implements I and yields the interface value in one step (the single-value form panics, so the comma-ok form is the query). The standard library is built on this: io.Copy asserts src.(WriterTo) and dst.(ReaderFrom) for its fast paths, and net/http documents Flusher, Hijacker and CloseNotifier as interfaces a ResponseWriter may additionally implement. What replaces the classic structure is the assertion plus interfaces that consumers declare and implementers satisfy implicitly - no registry, no cross-cast, no implementation change. The classic structure is still justified when the capability set is closed: a type switch over a small set of concrete types keeps the coverage explicit where an open interface would hide it.
pitfalls: The single-value assertion x.(I) panics when the capability is absent; for an optional interface the comma-ok form is mandatory.
A wrapper that implements only the base interface erases the optional ones it forwards - golang/go#21904 records the hand-written forwarding wrappers this forces on callers.

Interface satisfaction is structural: a type with a matching method set is accepted even when the semantics differ, and a typed nil pointer stored in a non-nil interface passes the assertion and then panics on use.
Asserting to a concrete type (x.(os.File)) tests provenance rather than capability - prefer an interface such as io.Seeker when only the operations are needed.
